# The Good Person and the Bad Person

*MN 113, the Sappurisa Sutta — set 3, Learning to Look at Your Own Mind*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 21 min · 3,699 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This discourse takes on a quiet problem in spiritual life: pride.

The Buddha goes through twenty-six things a monk might be proud of, one at a
time. Coming from a good family. Being well known. Receiving plenty of
support. Being learned, or an expert in the rules, or a good speaker. Living
in the forest, wearing rag robes, never lying down. Even reaching the deep
meditative states.

Each time, the *bad person* uses it to praise themselves and put others
down. The *good person* sees that none of it ends greed, aversion, or
delusion; what matters is how someone actually practices. For the meditative
states, the good person's answer goes further: the Buddha taught not to
identify even with these.

It ends with someone who has gone beyond all of it and no longer thinks of
anything as "me" at all.

## Translation

### The Setting

So I heard.

At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove,
Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Buddha addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus."

"Bhadante," the bhikkhus replied. The Buddha said this:

"Bhikkhus, I will teach you the qualities of a good person and the qualities
of a bad person. Listen and pay close attention. I will speak."

"Yes, Bhante," the bhikkhus replied. The Buddha said this:

### Family

"And what are the qualities of a bad person, bhikkhus? Bhikkhus, a bad person
has gone forth from a high family. They reflect: 'I have gone forth from a high
family, but these other bhikkhus have not.' Because of their high family, they
praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this is a quality of a bad
person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of a high family that qualities
of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone has not gone
forth from a high family, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of their high family. Bhikkhus, this is a quality of a good
person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person has gone forth from a great family. They
reflect: 'I have gone forth from a great family, but these other bhikkhus have
not.' Because of their great family, they praise themselves and put others
down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of a great family that qualities
of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone has not gone
forth from a great family, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of their great family. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good
person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person has gone forth from a very wealthy family.
They reflect: 'I have gone forth from a very wealthy family, but these other
bhikkhus have not.' Because of their very wealthy family, they praise
themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad
person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of a very wealthy family that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone has
not gone forth from a very wealthy family, if they practice in line with the
Dhamma, practice properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored
and praised for that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise
themselves or put others down because of their very wealthy family. Bhikkhus,
this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person has gone forth from an eminently wealthy
family. They reflect: 'I have gone forth from an eminently wealthy family, but
these other bhikkhus have not.' Because of their eminently wealthy family, they
praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad
person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of an eminently wealthy family
that qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone
has not gone forth from an eminently wealthy family, if they practice in line
with the Dhamma, practice properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are
honored and praised for that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise
themselves or put others down because of their eminently wealthy family.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

### Reputation and Gains

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person is well known and famous. They reflect: 'I
am well known and famous, but these other bhikkhus are unknown and of little
account.' Because of being well known, they praise themselves and put others
down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of being well known that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone is
not well known and famous, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of being well known. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good
person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person receives robes, alms food, lodgings, and
medicines and supplies for the sick. They reflect: 'I receive robes, alms food,
lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, but these other bhikkhus do
not.' Because of what they receive, they praise themselves and put others down.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of what someone receives that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone does
not receive robes, alms food, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the
sick, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice properly, and live in
line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for that.' Putting the
practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others down because of
what they receive. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

### Learning and Skill

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person is learned. They reflect: 'I am learned,
but these other bhikkhus are not.' Because of their learning, they praise
themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad
person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of learning that qualities of
greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone is not learned, if
they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice properly, and live in line with
the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for that.' Putting the practice first,
they do not praise themselves or put others down because of their learning.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person is an expert in the Vinaya. They reflect:
'I am an expert in the Vinaya, but these other bhikkhus are not.' Because of
their expertise in the Vinaya, they praise themselves and put others down.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of expertise in the Vinaya that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone is
not an expert in the Vinaya, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of their expertise in the Vinaya. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality
of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person is a speaker on the Dhamma. They reflect:
'I am a speaker on the Dhamma, but these other bhikkhus are not.' Because of
being a speaker on the Dhamma, they praise themselves and put others down.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of being a speaker on the Dhamma
that qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone
is not a speaker on the Dhamma, if they practice in line with the Dhamma,
practice properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and
praised for that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or
put others down because of being a speaker on the Dhamma. Bhikkhus, this too is
a quality of a good person.

### Ascetic Practices

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person lives in the forest. They reflect: 'I live
in the forest, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of living in the
forest, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a
quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of living in the forest that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone does
not live in the forest, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of living in the forest. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good
person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person wears rag robes. They reflect: 'I wear rag
robes, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of wearing rag robes, they
praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad
person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of wearing rag robes that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone does
not wear rag robes, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of wearing rag robes. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good
person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person eats only alms food. They reflect: 'I eat
only alms food, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of eating only alms
food, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a
quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of eating only alms food that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone does
not eat only alms food, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of eating only alms food. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a
good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person lives at the root of a tree. They reflect:
'I live at the root of a tree, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of
living at the root of a tree, they praise themselves and put others down.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of living at the root of a tree
that qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone
does not live at the root of a tree, if they practice in line with the Dhamma,
practice properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and
praised for that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or
put others down because of living at the root of a tree. Bhikkhus, this too is
a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person lives in a charnel ground. They reflect: 'I
live in a charnel ground, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of living
in a charnel ground, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this
too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of living in a charnel ground
that qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone
does not live in a charnel ground, if they practice in line with the Dhamma,
practice properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and
praised for that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or
put others down because of living in a charnel ground. Bhikkhus, this too is a
quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person lives in the open air. They reflect: 'I
live in the open air, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of living in
the open air, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is
a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of living in the open air that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone does
not live in the open air, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of living in the open air. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a
good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person never lies down. They reflect: 'I never lie
down, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of never lying down, they
praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad
person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of never lying down that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone is
not someone who never lies down, if they practice in line with the Dhamma,
practice properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and
praised for that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or
put others down because of never lying down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of
a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person sleeps wherever a bed is set out. They
reflect: 'I sleep wherever a bed is set out, but these other bhikkhus do not.'
Because of sleeping wherever a bed is set out, they praise themselves and put
others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of sleeping wherever a bed is
set out that qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if
someone does not sleep wherever a bed is set out, if they practice in line with
the Dhamma, practice properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are
honored and praised for that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise
themselves or put others down because of sleeping wherever a bed is set out.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person eats in one sitting. They reflect: 'I eat
in one sitting, but these other bhikkhus do not.' Because of eating in one
sitting, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a
quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'It is not because of eating in one sitting that
qualities of greed, aversion, or delusion come to an end. Even if someone does
not eat in one sitting, if they practice in line with the Dhamma, practice
properly, and live in line with the Dhamma, they are honored and praised for
that.' Putting the practice first, they do not praise themselves or put others
down because of eating in one sitting. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a
good person.

### Mental Themes and Formless Spheres

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded
from unwholesome dhammas, enters and remains in the first mental theme, with
thinking and pondering, with rejoicing and satisfaction born of seclusion. They
reflect: 'I have attained the first mental theme, but these other bhikkhus have
not.' Because of attaining the first mental theme, they praise themselves and
put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the first mental theme. For whatever they think it is,
it turns out otherwise.' Putting non-identification first, they do not praise
themselves or put others down because of attaining the first mental theme.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, with the subsiding of thinking and
pondering, with inner clarity and singleness of mind, enters and remains in the
second mental theme, without thinking and pondering, with rejoicing and
satisfaction born of unification. They reflect: 'I have attained the second
mental theme, but these other bhikkhus have not.' Because of attaining the
second mental theme, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus, this
too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the second mental theme. For whatever they think it is,
it turns out otherwise.' Putting non-identification first, they do not praise
themselves or put others down because of attaining the second mental theme.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, with the fading of rejoicing, remains in
dynamic balance, remembering and clearly knowing, experiences ease in the body,
and enters and remains in the third mental theme, of which the noble ones say:
"One of dynamic balance and remembering stays at ease". They reflect: 'I have
attained the third mental theme, but these other bhikkhus have not.' Because of
attaining the third mental theme, they praise themselves and put others down.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the third mental theme. For whatever they think it is,
it turns out otherwise.' Putting non-identification first, they do not praise
themselves or put others down because of attaining the third mental theme.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, with the abandoning of ease and
discomfort, and with the earlier ending of gladness and sadness, enters and
remains in the fourth mental theme, without discomfort and without ease,
purified by dynamic balance and remembering. They reflect: 'I have attained the
fourth mental theme, but these other bhikkhus have not.' Because of attaining
the fourth mental theme, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus,
this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the fourth mental theme. For whatever they think it is,
it turns out otherwise.' Putting non-identification first, they do not praise
themselves or put others down because of attaining the fourth mental theme.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, with the complete transcending of
recognitions of form, with the passing away of recognitions of resistance, with
non-attention to recognitions of diversity, aware that "space is boundless,"
enters and remains in the sphere of boundless space. They reflect: 'I have
attained the sphere of boundless space, but these other bhikkhus have not.'
Because of attaining the sphere of boundless space, they praise themselves and
put others down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the sphere of boundless space. For whatever they think
it is, it turns out otherwise.' Putting non-identification first, they do not
praise themselves or put others down because of attaining the sphere of
boundless space. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, going completely beyond the sphere of
boundless space, aware that "knowing is boundless," enters and remains in the
sphere of boundless knowing. They reflect: 'I have attained the sphere of
boundless knowing, but these other bhikkhus have not.' Because of attaining the
sphere of boundless knowing, they praise themselves and put others down.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the sphere of boundless knowing. For whatever they think
it is, it turns out otherwise.' Putting non-identification first, they do not
praise themselves or put others down because of attaining the sphere of
boundless knowing. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, going completely beyond the sphere of
boundless knowing, aware that "there is nothing at all," enters and remains in
the sphere of nothingness. They reflect: 'I have attained the sphere of
nothingness, but these other bhikkhus have not.' Because of attaining the
sphere of nothingness, they praise themselves and put others down. Bhikkhus,
this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the sphere of nothingness. For whatever they think it
is, it turns out otherwise.' Putting non-identification first, they do not
praise themselves or put others down because of attaining the sphere of
nothingness. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bad person, going completely beyond the sphere of
nothingness, enters and remains in the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition. They reflect: 'I have attained the
sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition, but these other bhikkhus
have not.' Because of attaining the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition, they praise themselves and put others
down. Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a bad person.

But a good person reflects: 'The Buddha has spoken of non-identification even
with the attainment of the sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition.
For whatever they think it is, it turns out otherwise.' Putting
non-identification first, they do not praise themselves or put others down
because of attaining the sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition.
Bhikkhus, this too is a quality of a good person.

### Beyond All Conceiving

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a good person, going completely beyond the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition, enters and remains in the cessation of
recognition and felt experience. When they see this with discernment, their
outflows are exhausted.

This bhikkhu does not think of anything, anywhere, or in any way."

That is what the Buddha said. The bhikkhus were glad and welcomed what the
Buddha had said.

The third discourse is finished.

<summary>Words used in this translation (30)</summary>
<dl>
<dt><dfn>aversion</dfn></dt>
<dd>One of the three &quot;roots&quot; behind unwholesome action, alongside greed and delusion -- the pushback against what&#x27;s unwanted or unpleasant.</dd>
<dt><dfn>Bhante</dfn></dt>
<dd>A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly &quot;venerable sir.&quot; Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhu</dfn></dt>
<dd>A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because &quot;monk&quot; carries centuries of unrelated European associations.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>body</dfn></dt>
<dd>The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.</dd>
<dt><dfn>born of seclusion</dfn></dt>
<dd>Coming from having stepped away from busyness and distraction, rather than from anything acquired.</dd>
<dt><dfn>cessation</dfn></dt>
<dd>The ending of dissatisfaction and its causes: what practice is finally for. Elsewhere on this site the same idea appears as &quot;quenching&quot;. Both render the same Pali word, &quot;nirodha&quot;, in different sentences.</dd>
<dt><dfn>clarity</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;amoha,&quot; literally &quot;non-delusion&quot; -- seeing without the confusion and distortion that drive harmful action.</dd>
<dt><dfn>clearly knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>Acting while plainly aware of what you are doing.</dd>
<dt><dfn>delusion</dfn></dt>
<dd>One of the three &quot;roots&quot; behind unwholesome action, alongside greed and aversion -- the confusion that keeps you from seeing what&#x27;s actually happening.</dd>
<dt><dfn>Dhamma</dfn></dt>
<dd>The Buddha&#x27;s teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.</dd>
<dt><dfn>dynamic balance</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;upekkhā&quot; (often translated &quot;equanimity&quot;) -- a steadiness that stays engaged rather than checking out, distinct from indifference.</dd>
<dt><dfn>fading</dfn></dt>
<dd>The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.</dd>
<dt><dfn>felt experience</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;vedanā&quot;, often translated &quot;feeling&quot;. It is the immediate pleasant, painful, or mixed tone of an experience, before any story we build on top of it.</dd>
<dt><dfn>form</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;rūpa&quot; -- the physical, material aspect of experience, one of the five heaps.</dd>
<dt><dfn>gladness</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;muditā&quot;, often translated &quot;sympathetic joy&quot;. It means being truly glad at someone else&#x27;s good fortune. You cultivate it as a practice; you do not assume it comes naturally.</dd>
<dt><dfn>greed</dfn></dt>
<dd>One of the three &quot;roots&quot; behind unwholesome action, alongside aversion and delusion -- the acquisitive pull toward what looks satisfying.</dd>
<dt><dfn>knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;viññāṇa&quot; (often translated &quot;consciousness&quot;) -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>mental theme</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jhāna&quot; -- a single theme the mind rests on and holds steadily. Described in a sequence of four, each calmer than the last. Most translations leave the word in Pāli.</dd>
<dt><dfn>outflows</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;āsavā&quot; -- deep-running habits that keep seeping out and driving behaviour, classically sensuality, becoming, and ignorance. Often translated &quot;taints&quot; or &quot;defilements.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>recognition</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saññā&quot; (often translated &quot;perception&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.</dd>
<dt><dfn>rejoicing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;pīti&quot; (often translated &quot;rapture&quot;) -- the bright, uplifted gladness that shows up when practice is going well.</dd>
<dt><dfn>remembering</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;sati&quot;. It means actively keeping what matters in mind and coming back to it when you lose it. It is not bare attention to whatever happens to be present.</dd>
<dt><dfn>resistance</dfn></dt>
<dd>A reflexive pushing-away from what&#x27;s unwanted, arising automatically in response to unpleasant feeling.</dd>
<dt><dfn>singleness of mind</dfn></dt>
<dd>The mind become single and undivided as thinking and pondering settle in the second mental theme. Kept distinct from unification of mind (samādhi).</dd>
<dt><dfn>sphere of boundless knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on knowing itself without limit.</dd>
<dt><dfn>sphere of boundless space</dfn></dt>
<dd>A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on space without limit.</dd>
<dt><dfn>sphere of nothingness</dfn></dt>
<dd>A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on there being nothing at all to take up.</dd>
<dt><dfn>unification</dfn></dt>
<dd>Short for unification of mind (samādhi) inside a longer phrase, such as &quot;born of unification&quot; or &quot;the faculty of unification.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>unwholesome</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;akusala&quot;. Roughly: mentally and ethically harmful. It is blameworthy, leads to harm, and people with good judgment criticize it.</dd>
</dl>
</details>

*[aversion]: One of the three "roots" behind unwholesome action, alongside greed and delusion -- the pushback against what's unwanted or unpleasant.
*[Bhante]: A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly "venerable sir." Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.
*[bhikkhu]: A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because "monk" carries centuries of unrelated European associations.
*[bhikkhus]: Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha's usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly "friends" in force.
*[body]: The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.
*[born of seclusion]: Coming from having stepped away from busyness and distraction, rather than from anything acquired.
*[cessation]: The ending of dissatisfaction and its causes: what practice is finally for. Elsewhere on this site the same idea appears as "quenching". Both render the same Pali word, "nirodha", in different sentences.
*[clarity]: This project's rendering of "amoha," literally "non-delusion" -- seeing without the confusion and distortion that drive harmful action.
*[clearly knowing]: Acting while plainly aware of what you are doing.
*[delusion]: One of the three "roots" behind unwholesome action, alongside greed and aversion -- the confusion that keeps you from seeing what's actually happening.
*[Dhamma]: The Buddha's teaching taken as a whole -- both what he taught and the way things actually are, which the teaching describes.
*[dynamic balance]: This project's rendering of "upekkhā" (often translated "equanimity") -- a steadiness that stays engaged rather than checking out, distinct from indifference.
*[fading]: The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.
*[felt experience]: This project's rendering of "vedanā", often translated "feeling". It is the immediate pleasant, painful, or mixed tone of an experience, before any story we build on top of it.
*[form]: This project's rendering of "rūpa" -- the physical, material aspect of experience, one of the five heaps.
*[gladness]: This project's rendering of "muditā", often translated "sympathetic joy". It means being truly glad at someone else's good fortune. You cultivate it as a practice; you do not assume it comes naturally.
*[greed]: One of the three "roots" behind unwholesome action, alongside aversion and delusion -- the acquisitive pull toward what looks satisfying.
*[knowing]: This project's rendering of "viññāṇa" (often translated "consciousness") -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.
*[mental theme]: This project's rendering of "jhāna" -- a single theme the mind rests on and holds steadily. Described in a sequence of four, each calmer than the last. Most translations leave the word in Pāli.
*[outflows]: This project's rendering of "āsavā" -- deep-running habits that keep seeping out and driving behaviour, classically sensuality, becoming, and ignorance. Often translated "taints" or "defilements."
*[recognition]: This project's rendering of "saññā" (often translated "perception") -- the mind's act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.
*[rejoicing]: This project's rendering of "pīti" (often translated "rapture") -- the bright, uplifted gladness that shows up when practice is going well.
*[remembering]: This project's rendering of "sati". It means actively keeping what matters in mind and coming back to it when you lose it. It is not bare attention to whatever happens to be present.
*[resistance]: A reflexive pushing-away from what's unwanted, arising automatically in response to unpleasant feeling.
*[singleness of mind]: The mind become single and undivided as thinking and pondering settle in the second mental theme. Kept distinct from unification of mind (samādhi).
*[sphere of boundless knowing]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on knowing itself without limit.
*[sphere of boundless space]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on space without limit.
*[sphere of nothingness]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on there being nothing at all to take up.
*[unification]: Short for unification of mind (samādhi) inside a longer phrase, such as "born of unification" or "the faculty of unification."
*[unwholesome]: This project's rendering of "akusala". Roughly: mentally and ethically harmful. It is blameworthy, leads to harm, and people with good judgment criticize it.
